newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Heineken shares fall on analyst downgrades.
newsitem.headline: Heineken shares fall on analyst downgrades.

text.p: The stock of Dutch brewer Heineken NV fell to a seven-month low Monday, driven down by a spate of downgrades after last week's shock profit warning, with analysts predicting more falls to come.

Heineken shares have plunged 16 percent, losing 58.70 guilders to 304.00 after last Friday's news of lower-than-expected first-half profits and its warning that 1996 profits would fall short of 1995's 664 million guilders ($392 million).
"It will go lower," said John David Roeg, analyst at Labouchere, adding he had downgraded the stock to a Sell from a Hold.

"It could go as low as 250.00 to 275.00 guilders by the end of the year, perhaps sooner," said Roeg. The stock hit an all-time high of 402.00 guilders in June, almost doubling in the 14 months from April 1995.

Heineken was at the forefront of this year's Amsterdam stocks surge, climbing on its perceived growth prospects, which were punctured by a statement from chairman Karel Vuursteen Friday that the 10 percent annual gains investors had enjoyed over the past six years could not be guaranteed.
Volume in Heineken shares has ballooned from the usual 200,000 to 400,000 a day, with one million changing hands by Monday afternoon. Over 3.7 million were traded on Friday.
Analysts warned even more froth would be blown off the shares, taking their drop earlier Monday below 300.00 guilders to a seven-month low of 294.00 guilders.
The problem for the international brewer lies in a saturated European beer market, where Heineken racks up over 70 percent of its sales at present.

With cooler summer weather this year hitting consumption, sales will be particularly hard hit in 1996. But analysts agreed that Heineken's leading market position in many European countries, recent acquisitions in France, which are expected to contribute to net profit in around three years, and strong investment in South East Asia mean the brewer's problems may be relatively short-lived.

"My feeling is the long-term story for Heineken is still a very good one," said MeesPierson analyst Darrell Duthie. "They have a very strong position in European markets, their investments in Asia are going apace and they're in a good position in the U.S."
